lessons.title: Recurrence, BPTT and vanishing gradients
lessons.intro: A recurrent network reads a sequence one step at a time and carries a hidden state, using the same weights at every step. Training it means unrolling that loop and backpropagating through time. This lesson shows the shapes, why the gradient fades or explodes with distance, and the one fix every practitioner uses for the exploding case.
takeaways: Same weights every step: parameters independent of T, compute and activation memory linear in T.
dL/dh_k = product of per-step Jacobians; norm shrinks or grows exponentially with distance.
Gradient for a shared weight = sum over time steps.
Clip the global norm for exploding gradients; vanishing needs gates, good init or shortcut paths.
lessons.trap: Expecting gradient clipping to fix 'the model forgets the start of the sequence'. Clipping bounds big gradients; the forgetting comes from vanishing ones.

sections.heading: The loop and the shared weights
sections.text: h_t = tanh(W_xh x_t + W_hh h_(t-1) + b). The parameter count does not depend on the sequence length, but the work does: each step needs the previous one, so training is sequential in time.
code: print('params', h * d + h * h + h)
Wx, Wh = rng.normal(0, 0.5, (h, d)), rng.normal(0, 0.3, (h, h))

sections.heading: Backprop through time is a product
sections.text: Unrolled, the gradient of the last state with respect to an early state is a product of one Jacobian per step. If each factor has size below 1 the product vanishes exponentially; above 1 it explodes. Watch both with a scalar recurrence.

sections.heading: A hand-checkable gradient
sections.text: For the linear recurrence h_t = w h_(t-1) + x_t the shared weight collects one term per step, and an input k steps back reaches the loss multiplied by w^k. Verify such derivations with finite differences, as the Forge Lab does.
code: print(round((last(0.5 + e, xs) - last(0.5 - e, xs)) / (2 * e), 6))

sections.heading: Clip exploding gradients
sections.text: Rescale the global gradient norm when it exceeds a limit: the direction is kept and the step is bounded. This stops loss spikes but cannot revive a vanished signal.

lessons.title: Gates, seq2seq and the attention bottleneck
lessons.intro: LSTM and GRU cells make the state update additive and learned, which keeps a gradient path open across many steps. Sequence-to-sequence models built on them hit a different wall: the whole source had to fit in one vector. Attention removed it and led to transformers.
takeaways: Cell path: d c_t / d c_(t-1) = f; start forget biases positive so the gate begins near 1.
GRU: 3 gate blocks, LSTM: 4; check the library's gate convention.
Teacher forcing speeds training and causes exposure bias; mask padding everywhere.
A single context vector is a bottleneck; attention is a learned weighted average of all encoder states.
lessons.trap: Saying 'LSTMs solve vanishing gradients'. They make long paths trainable but the gate must stay near 1, and very long contexts are still hard, which is why attention won.

sections.heading: The LSTM cell path
sections.text: c_t = f c_(t-1) + i g. Along the cell the derivative is the forget gate itself, so a gate near 1 passes the gradient almost unchanged. Compare with a squashing recurrence.

sections.heading: The GRU gate and the cost
sections.text: A GRU uses an update gate to interpolate between the old state and a candidate, with a reset gate that decides how much past to use when forming the candidate. It has three gate blocks instead of four.
code: print([((1 - z) * h_prev + z * cand).tolist() for z in (0.0, 0.5, 1.0)])

sections.heading: Encoder, decoder and teacher forcing
sections.text: The encoder compresses the source into a state, the decoder generates the target token by token. Training feeds the true previous token (teacher forcing); at inference the model eats its own output, so errors can compound. Batches are padded, so every mean, loss and softmax needs a mask.

sections.heading: Attention removes the bottleneck
sections.text: Instead of one fixed vector the decoder takes a weighted average of all encoder states, with weights from a softmax over similarity scores. The same step, applied between all positions of one sequence, is self-attention.

lessons.title: Embeddings and contrastive learning
lessons.intro: Models cannot consume words, only numbers. An embedding table turns token ids into trainable vectors whose geometry reflects usage. This lesson covers lookup, similarity measures, how skip-gram with negative sampling trains vectors cheaply, and the InfoNCE loss behind contrastive training.
takeaways: Embedding = row lookup; equal to one-hot @ E.
Cosine ignores length; with unit vectors dot = cosine.
SGNS: one positive plus k sampled negatives with sigmoids instead of a full softmax.
InfoNCE = cross-entropy over (positive + negatives); temperature and false negatives are the knobs and the risks.
lessons.trap: Judging an embedding model by its training loss alone. Evaluate on the task it serves (retrieval recall, clustering purity) and look for false negatives and duplicates in the data.

sections.heading: Lookup is a one-hot multiply
sections.text: An embedding layer indexes a table E of shape (vocab, dim). It equals multiplying a one-hot vector by E, but costs a row read, and only the used rows get gradient.

sections.heading: Cosine or dot product
sections.text: Cosine ignores vector length, the dot product does not. Normalise embeddings first and the two coincide, which is why retrieval systems often store unit vectors.
code: print('cosine', round(float(a @ b / np.linalg.norm(a) / np.linalg.norm(b)), 4), 'dot', float(a @ b))
u, v = a / np.linalg.norm(a), b / np.linalg.norm(b)

sections.heading: Skip-gram with negative sampling
sections.text: Predict context words from a centre word. A full softmax over the vocabulary is too slow, so each real pair is scored against a few random negatives with a sigmoid. The idea (not the exact recipe) lives on in modern embedding training.
code: pairs = [(toks[i], toks[j]) for i in range(5) for j in range(max(0, i - 1), min(5, i + 2)) if j != i]

sections.heading: InfoNCE and temperature
sections.text: Contrastive learning pulls an anchor towards its positive and away from the other items in the batch: a softmax cross-entropy where the positive is the right answer. The temperature sets how much weight the hardest negatives get.
